text:
1
INTRODUCTION
1. This United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) provides an
analysis of ways in which United Nations funds, programmes and specialised agencies in
Romania (collectively referred to as “organisations”) can increase convergence in their
programmes in order to more effectively utilise UN system resources and better
complement and reinforce their activities. It was produced by the UN Country Team in
Romania, with the expectation that it will be a useful tool to optimise the collective impact
of their various programmes. Romania was among 11 countries included in an initial pilot
exercise to initiate this new concept.
2. The present document will describe the process of preparation of the UNDAF and
the participants involved, outline the current development context in Romania, and set forth
the objectives and strategies which will unite the various UN organisations in supporting
Romania’s development effort.
1. THE PREPARATION OF THE UNITED NATIONS DEVELOPMENT
ASSISTANCE FRAMEWORK FOR ROMANIA
 a. The Process:
3. Upon receipt of the provisional guidelines in September l997, the UN Resident
Coordinator informed the Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of the UNDAF
exercise and briefed relevant government agencies about the preparation process. Their
feedback was positive, and some of the main government counterparts of the different UN
organizations worked together on the Common Country Assessment (CCA) exercise.
4. The preparation of the CCA started in September l997 with a status report on
Romania’s follow-up to the UN Global Conferences. A methodology for the preparation
of the CCA was then developed with the help of two UNDAF facilitators provided by UN
Headquarters. As a first step, all participating organisations contributed indicators and data
to a common data base which was formatted and screened for consistency. Thematic issues
for the CCA were identified in a general brainstorming meeting and assigned to individuals
for the drafting of briefs, which provided a description and analysis of specific problems
supported by quantitative and qualitative data, followed by an assessment. The briefs were
further developed in thematic groups and in the general Country Team meetings and used
as a basis for the preparation of a first draft.
5. Since January 1998 every chapter of the CCA have been subjected to in-depth
reviews by inter-organisation teams, in consultation with representatives from government,
civil society and selected donor agencies. A final draft was produced in April 1998.2
6. The thorough preparation of the CCA crystallised participants’ ideas for the
UNDAF, which therefore required a relatively short time to prepare. All participating UN
organisations were invited to provide their own inputs in accordance with the agreed
UNDAF outline. These were discussed in regular meetings between the participants
throughout the process. A first draft of the UNDAF was produced in late May and
distributed to UN headquarters, the Romanian Government and donors. Meetings were held
with the Prime Minister and other senior government officials and a number of donors, who
unanimously supported the exercise and whose comments were taken into account in the
preparation of the final draft. This was completed and signed by the UN Country Team at
the end of June.
b. The Participants:
The UN Country Team
7. The following UN organisations represented in Romania participated in the Country
Team, through their representatives and liaison officers: ILO, UNAIDS, UNDP, UNESCO,
UNFPA, UNHCR, UNICEF, and WHO.
UN organisations not represented in the country:
8. An effort was made to include other UN organisations without an in-country
presence in Romania. Of these, UNCTAD, ITC and particularly FAO provided inputs.
Government
9. Governmental partners participated actively in the preparation of the CCA, in a
supportive and ongoing dialogue with the UN Country Team. Initially, meetings took place
with the Prime Minister and other key Ministers and Parliamentarians, to inform them of
the exercise. Participating governmental bodies included the Office of the Prime Minister,
the Ministries of Foreign Affairs, Labour and Social Protection, Education, Interior,
Finance, and the following institutions:

10. A special effort was made to include civil society, particularly through NGO’s.
While most of these are still of recent vintage in Romania, several participated actively in
the process. They included:

c. Lessons from Experience
11. Since the preparation of the UNDAF is of a pilot nature both in Romania and
worldwide, the experience of the participants may be of interest for future exercises. Their
reactions and observations are summarised below:
- While the exercise in Romania was of a pilot nature, participants felt that,
considering the extensive involvement of government and civil society, it
created a serious commitment on the part of the UN system to actually make
effective use of the CCA and UNDAF as instruments for collaborative
programming.
- The preparation of the CCA and UNDAF has provided all members of the
UN team a unique opportunity to work together in a sustained manner over a
significant period of time. It also allowed the UN leadership in the country to
coordinate an important inter-organisation effort and gain valuable
experience.
- Because of unfamiliarity with this type of inter-organisation effort, the
preparation of the CCA took a relatively long time. Much of this time was
well spent in terms of generating important information, facilitating4
interaction, and laying the groundwork for future exercises. However, in the
case of several of the staff involved, it constituted a significant additional
burden.
- The support of the facilitators would have been more useful if it had come at
the beginning of the exercise. It would also have been desirable for them to
maintain contact with the inter-organisation team after their visit, to provide
follow-up and further backstopping as necessary.
- The inter-organisation teams functioned well, at the supervisory and working
group levels, and the leadership of the Resident Coordinator was essential.
- The availability of a well structured, reliable and consistent data base should
significantly speed up the next UNDAF exercise. It is important to consider
this as the first stage of a continuing and dynamic process of collecting,
processing and updating data supported by appropriate research and analysis.
- A more fully developed set of UNDAF guidelines, which clarify mechanisms
of implementation, will significantly assist the preparation process in other
countries.
- The UN Country Team believes that active involvement of the Bretton
Woods institutions in the UNDAF process is very important, especially for
countries in transition, like Romania. Despite the best efforts of the UN
Country Team, it was not possible to actively involve the Bretton Woods
institutions in the UNDAF as a concept. However, there has been and
continues to be regular consultation between the UN organisations and the
World Bank. Several of these discussions relate to the relationship between
UNDAF objectives and social development priorities reflected in the World
Bank Development Assistance Strategy.
2. MAJOR DEVELOPMENT CHALLENGES FACING ROMANIA
a. Summary of National Development Goals
12. Romania entered a new historical era in l990 when it began the transformation from
a highly centralised command economy to a market economy. The far-reaching economic
and social changes required for the transition have proved to be difficult, placing a heavy
burden on the population.
13. After an initial gradualist approach which failed to achieve the projected results, a
new, accelerated and far-reaching reform programme was initiated in early l997. This5
programme aimed at correcting the growing macro-economic and structural imbalances in
the economy and providing the basis for sustainable, poverty-reducing growth over the
longer term. In this connection, four interconnected priority goals were identified:
- promoting structural reform and private sector development;
- redefining and improving the role of the state;
- fighting poverty and developing human capital;
- protecting and enhancing the environment;
14. The principal policies used to respond to these priorities were outlined in some
detail in the Government’s Basic Programme for Macroeconomic Stabilisation and
Development until the Year 2000, which was published in December l996. This document
served as a basic Government statement, in the absence of a Country Strategy Note. It
identifies ten areas for action:
- ensuring macro-economic stability and consolidating the system of financial
markets;
- outward orientation of the economy, especially with a view to Romania’s
integration in the European Union;
- consolidating the competitive mechanisms for distributing resources in the
economy and developing the private sector;
- industrial restructuring and local, regional and rural development;
- ensuring durable development of agriculture;
- developing infrastructure;
- enhancing efficiency of the utilization of natural capital;
- enhancing efficiency of investments in human capital and modernising the
social protection system;
- modernising the public administration system and increasing the efficiency of
the production of public goods;
- stimulating the development of civil society and consolidating social dialogue.
15. One of Romania’s principal challenges has been to limit the negative effects of
accelerated economic reform on the quality of life of the people. One manifestation is the
significant increase in poverty, which now effects about 25% of the population. In its
1998-2000 programme the Government is undertaking measures to combat poverty,
including the establishment of a Poverty Alleviation Committee, development of a national
strategy to prevent and alleviate poverty, and improvements to the system of social6
allowances. It also envisages a review of programmes in education and health care to make
them respond better to the needs of the poorer segments of the population, as well as new
programmes of income generation, rural development and other activities to strengthen the
position of the poor. Greater involvement of NGO’s, international financial institutions and
development organisations is contributing to this process.
16. The CCA underlines the importance of these reforms. It also recommends special
attention to measures that benefit vulnerable groups, particularly children, and strengthen
the position of women in society.
b. Follow- up to UN Summits and Conventions
17. Romania participated in all of the major UN Global Conferences over the last
decade. Follow-up action to a number of them has been undertaken, but generally this has
not been pursued in a systematic and sustained manner. As explained earlier, the
Government’s priorities have been focused largely in the economic sphere, sometimes at
the expense of other areas of concern.
18. The following is a brief description of follow-up efforts with respect to the various
conferences:
- World Summit for Children. The President of Romania participated in the
Conference and Romania ratified the Convention on the Rights of the Child at
an early date. The National Plan of Action for Children was prepared in
October 1994 and approved by the Government in October 1995. Achievement
of Summit goals is monitored on an annual basis. Current priorities have caused
some delay in the implementation of the National Plan of Action.
- UN Conference on Environment and Development. Romania was a signatory
to the Conference decisions. A National Biodiversity Strategy and National
Environmental Action Plan were prepared with the assistance of UNDP, the
World Bank and EU Phare. A framework law on environmental protection was
prepared in 1995. In close collaboration with WHO, a National Environmental
Health Action Plan was produced. A multi-sectoral commission was established
to monitor implementation.
- World Conference on Human Rights. Romania signed the Vienna Declaration
on Human Rights. It has also ratified the European Convention for the
protection of Human Rights and the additional protocols.
- International Conference on Population and Development. The Conference
Programme of Action was signed by Romania. There is no designated
institutional body for the coordination of population programmes and policy7
preparation. However, a department was created in the National Commission
for Statistics whose role is to analyse and monitor population issues.
- Fourth World Conference on Women. The Conference Declaration was signed
and ratified and an Action Plan was drafted by the Ministry of Labour.
- World Summit for Social Development. Romania signed the declaration and
commitments made at the Summit were reflected in the “Basic Programme for
Romania’s Macroeconomic Stability and Development until year 2000”.
- Second UN Conference on Human Settlements. Romania signed the Istanbul
Declaration. It produced a National Report “The Sustainable Development of
Human Settlements and a Decent Home for Everyone”. It also established a
focal point under the Ministry of Public Works and Land-use Planning for
follow-up to the Conference.
- World Food Summit. Romania participated but no information on follow-up is
available
- Conference on Education for All. Romania signed the convention. Neither a
national plan of action nor follow-up mechanisms were established. Some
recommendations of the conference are reflected in the Government’s national
programme.
19. Generally speaking, systematic congruence between Romania’s national priorities
and those formulated at the Global Conferences is still lacking. To promote follow-up,
there may be a need for more intensive UN advocacy and awareness raising, to remind the
authorities and civil society of the importance and relevance of Romania’s commitments.
This will be an important part of UNDAF implementation. It will also indirectly help to
fulfill the requirements for accession to the European Union, which is one of Romania’s
top policy objectives.
3. SUMMARY OF THE COMMON COUNTRY ASSESSMENT (CCA)
a. Review of Main CCA Indicators.
20. The starting point for socio-economic and political transformation in Romania, in
1989, was precarious compared to other countries in Central and Eastern Europe. Thus,
while in a sense the transformation to a democratic society with a market-based economy
has been more dramatic, it has also been more problematic. Nonetheless, Romania has
made great efforts to overcome longstanding problems such as political centralisation,
economic inefficiency, limited citizen participation, and insufficient attention to important8
elements of sustainable human development such as health care, education, gender
equality, participatory democracy, and environmental protection. International
commitments made by Romania in these fields, as well as political reform, economic
liberalisation, and the development of civil society, are evidence of real progress. Yet, as
mentioned above, the social costs of transition have been extremely high, exacerbated by
economic problems, and “growing pains” within the emerging multi-party political system.
21. Regarding human rights, the UN system has started to adopt a more multi-faceted
and holistic approach. This has potentially great significance for Romania, enabling it to
complement and move beyond its progress related to more traditional civil and political
rights (as enshrined in international treaties) to a renewed focus on social, economic, and
cultural rights. In accordance with UN principles and the concept of sustainable human
development, these rights apply to the whole of society including vulnerable groups like
women, children, minorities, the elderly, pensioners, the disabled, and refugees, and relate
to the need for their empowerment and participation. With respect to the rights of children,
the Government has actively followed-up on the 1990 Summit for Children and the
Convention on the Rights of the Child, although recently there have been delays in
reporting to the committee on the rights of the child under the CRC implementation.
22. In December 1996 the Government published its 1997-2000 Governance
Programme. It set out broad guidelines for institutional reform in Romania. These involved
strengthening the role of Parliament and reform of the Executive, strengthening the rule of
law and accountability, decentralisation, and local autonomy. It included a new social
partnership with civil society. Progress towards these goals has been impeded by a number
of problems, and tends to be slow in several areas. External assistance can help to speed up
some of these processes. In April 1998 the new Government issued its Programme for
1998-2000, which for the most part continues to reflect these priorities.
23. Statistics indicate that despite the commitments made by Romania at the World
Summit for Social Development, poverty has become an increasingly serious problem.
According to some estimates, close to one-fourth of the population lives at or below the
subsistence level of approximately $ 3/day established for the CEE region. Some 17.7% of
the population lives on less than the universal standard of $1/day/person (absolute
poverty), while 15% of the population earns or receives a pension of less than $1/day.
Also, the gap between rich and poor has increased significantly. The average income per
person from the highest household income quintile is four times higher than the poorest
quintile. The richest ten percent have five times the income of the poorest. Poverty most
severely affects rural inhabitants, women, families with children, and the elderly. Faster
and more equitable privatisation, and the creation of a suitable enabling environment for
small business (streamlined legal framework, access to credit, reduced bureaucracy), are
positive steps which have recently been taken to improve economic performance and9
reduce unemployment and poverty.
24. The status of health care in Romania can be evaluated in the context of a number of
UN Global Conferences, notably those on Population, Food and Nutrition, and the WHO
Health for All Strategy, to which Romania has subscribed. Statistics indicate that Romania
has some of the highest abortion and infant and maternal mortality rates in Europe, and
decreasing life expectancy.

Also, the health sector suffers from under funding and low salaries and morale on the part
of health-care workers. At the same time, significant reforms to the health care system are
underway, to improve efficiency and emphasise primary care. Amongst current priorities
are controlling communicable and sexually transmitted diseases, and efforts to combat
malnutrition, poor sanitation, and problems associated with unsafe food and drinking water
(which are increasing).
25. Standards in the field of education are derived from the World Conference on
Education for All, the International Conference on Adult Education, and the Beijing
Conference. Accordingly, the Education Law of 1995 shifts orientation of the framework
from administration to content. The proportion of GDP devoted to this cause is not
sufficient, as there is a shortage of educational materials, a tendency towards greater
truancy and non-attendance, and declining quality of educational facilities. Other issues
deserving greater attention are teacher re-training, curricula development, introduction of
sex education in the curricula, and the disparity between rural and urban education.
26. In environment, Romania is actively participating in the UN Framework
Convention on Climate Change, the Montreal Protocol, the Convention on Biological10
Diversity, and follow-up to the UN Conference on Environment and Development. A
National Bio-diversity Strategy and Environmental Action Plan are designed to protect
some of the significant and unique natural resources in Romania. On the other hand, there
is a long legacy of environmental problems from decades of heavy yet energy inefficient
industrialisation, without regard to pollution. Both air and water resources suffer from
high levels of contamination, which has a measurable effect upon the health and quality of
life of many Romanian citizens (see the National Environmental Health Action Plan).
b. Implications for the UNDAF
27. As indicated above, the CCA reveals that the gap between current conditions in
Romania and many of the goals set forth in international agreements and at the Global
Conferences is increasing, and that Romania is falling further behind many of its
neighbours in this regard. Clearly, the multi-faceted nature of the transition process and
the daunting array of challenges facing Romania necessitate an integrated and
comprehensive approach, which brings together the diverse actors who can and should
participate. In this regard, the CCA lays the groundwork for an UNDAF process which
will enable the UN system to a) serve as a catalyst and a facilitator, and b) offer technical
and substantive expertise in crucial areas of focus.
28. In the first capacity, the UN system can help ensure that all of the interested parties
are included in a consultative process designed to identify, develop, and implement the
most appropriate strategies and activities. In particular, civil society in its widest sense
must become an active participant. Better governance is the strategic objective, which will
subsequently promote many aspects of sustainable human development.
29. With regard to technical and substantive expertise, the CCA helps identify the wide
range of assistance the UN needs to bring to Romania via the UNDAF. On the basis of the
CCA, the UNDAF will enable the UN to weave its expertise into a more coordinated
framework, and build upon the comparative advantages that the various UN organisations
offer. Thus, the information in the CCA will enable the UN system, via the UNDAF, to
combine efforts in a synergistic fashion for the strategic benefit of Romania, and make the
best use of comparative advantages such as rapid response time, in-country presence,
neutrality, comprehensive information resources, institutional knowledge, experience with
transition issues in numerous countries, and ability to build local capacity.
4. THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM IN ROMANIA
a. The Current Role of the United Nations System
30. During the l980s several UN organisations - IAEA, ILO, IMF, UNDP, UNESCO,
UNIDO and WHO - provided multilateral technical cooperation to Romania. At that time11
the role of the UN in-country focused on the provision of high-level technical assistance,
overseas training for scientific and technical experts, and the procurement of equipment
which at that time was not otherwise available. The main areas of activity were science and
technology, higher education, management, agriculture, industry, transport, energy,
telecommunications and health.
31. After the 1989 Revolution and the ensuing changes in the national political,
economic, social and cultural situation, the UN system was able to assume a more dynamic
role in supporting Romanian development. At that time other UN organisations – UNFPA,
UNHCR and UNICEF – opened offices and commenced operations; ILO and WHO
established liaison offices.
32. The changed development assistance priorities after the Revolution and the
congruence between some of Romania’s needs during the transition process and UN areas
of comparative advantage brought about a significant shift in the emphasis of UN
programmes from the economic to the social sector. This was critical, since the negative
consequences of the economic changes had their heaviest impact on those least equipped to
withstand the full strength of the new market forces. At the same time there was a growing
place for strategic UN support in the areas of policy development, environmental
protection, governance, democracy, and the promotion of civil society.
33. Immediately after the Revolution, when few other sources of outside assistance
were available, the presence of the UN system was a strategic factor in the country’s
development. After the European Union, the World Bank, and other donors arrived and
started their own programmes, the UN role was reduced and became even more focused on
social issues. This trend was reinforced by the conclusions reached at the various UN
Global Conferences, which added to the authority of the UN system in Romania in the
social field. This is evidenced by such developments as the establishment of the National
Commission on the Prevention and Alleviation of Poverty and the initiation of strategic
planning on HIV/AIDS, which were achieved with strong encouragement and support from
the UN system. Another example is the National Plan of Action for Children which was
approved by the Government in October 1995. At the same time, progress in making these
plans and institutions operational has been slow.
34. Since the beginning of the transition, the UN system has been focusing especially
on the human dimension, through capacity and institution building. It is working with the
Government and civil society to promote sustainable human development and improve
basic living conditions. The combined UN assistance is currently focused on:
- alleviation of poverty;
- improved access to information and services concerning modern family
planning methods and reproductive health care;12
- improved educational services, including family education;
- promotion of human rights in their widest sense;
- promotion of employment and social security;
- promotion of the rights of children, especially those in difficult
circumstances;
- improved access to primary health care and services, particularly for
women and children;
- promotion of women’s role in society and gender equity;
- protection of environmental and natural resources and promotion of
their sustainable use;
- promotion of sustainable livelihoods through strengthening of small and
medium size enterprises and restructuring of privatised enterprises;
- strengthening democracy, transparent and accountable governance,
citizen participation and civil society development;
- prevention of HIV/AIDS, and integration of preventive measures into
reproductive health care;
- protection of refugee rights;
- prevention and reduction of statelessness;
35. The UN effort in Romania aims at assisting the Government to promote a new
culture of development, stressing human rights, poverty alleviation, integration of
democratic and social elements into reform strategies, and achievement of long-term
human well-being. This is particularly appropriate at a time when the Government is
mainly focused on economic issues, at the possible expense of social ones. It also enables
the UN to fill a crucial niche, utilising its special expertise for the benefit of Romania.
36. Careful targeting of UN cooperation has become increasingly important, in view of
the significant number of other donors providing support. It has become critical to have
clearly defined programmes with effective coordination between UN organisations,
whether or not represented in Romania, and to have common or coordinated advocacy
positions that clearly define the target population and institutions for UN capacity building
exercises in Romania. This requires a well-structured dialogue with the Government of
Romania to stress the potential benefits from a strengthened partnership with the UN, and
placing Romania within the framework of global programmes and new paradigms being
established through a reformed UN system.13
b. Lessons from Experience
37. In carrying out their diverse activities and programmes the various UN
organisations have reached, over the years, a number of strategic and operational
conclusions based on their collective experience in Romania. Some key examples are:
- In spite of the very limited resources available to the UN system, its
assistance can have a relatively major impact when focused on strategic areas,
and when linked to or formulated in consideration of the interests, capabilities
and activities of other international donors.
- Activities to promote national capacity-building have proved to be effective
in the development of sustainable expertise, institutions and methods. Sound
process is an important component of good product. This includes capacity
building for NGOs through support for activities, training and networking.
- Sustainability of political will is as important as initial steps in the correct
direction. A lesson can be drawn from the National Plan of Action (NPA) for
Children, approved by the Government in October 1995. The NPA received
neither sufficient funding nor operational support at the start. The complexity
of the task as well as coordination challenges resulted in a very ambitious
project, whose success depends not only on technical quality, but also on
changing political environment and will.
- The neutral status and catalytic role of UN organisations can make a
significant difference. The ability to bring together partners; governmental
authorities and NGO’s, local and city councils, donors and fundraisers,
cooperating agencies and counterparts, interested individuals and institutions,
constitutes one of the UN system’s significant comparative advantages.
- Some of the most successful strategies for programme delivery have been
models of excellence and pilot projects. Education, training, exposure to
international contacts and experience, and networking have had a great
multiplier effect, in many cases producing new initiatives, improved delivery
of services, and the extension of activities.
- Small projects constitute an effective means for responding to specific
governmental priorities not covered by other donors.
- The global Human Development Reports have been instrumental in raising
awareness of the human dimension of development. Meanwhile, the national
Human Development Reports have promoted novel approaches to
development policy issues by providing a new and updated data base which14
highlights important elements of development issues in Romania.
- There is a need for a better information dissemination effort with respect to
the UN programmes and activities in Romania. Mention of the UN sometimes
raises excessive expectations, particularly financial. On the other hand, the
advantages and potential of the various services rendered by the UN system
are not always sufficiently known, appreciated and utilised.
- From the perspective of individual UN organisations it was found that in
many cases coordination and intersectoriality were important components of a
successful programme. At the same time, no mechanisms were normally
available to facilitate activities in which several organisations were involved,
leaving solutions to problems to be improvised locally.
- The experience of recent years as well as the preparation of the present
UNDAF itself points to the potential for UN organisations in Romania to
further develop links between their programmes and offices. Closer
cooperation, programme coordination and information sharing will generate
increased impact and efficiency.
38. The various lessons learned, while not equally applicable to all programmes or
organisations, do suggest directions and modalities which will most enhance the
effectiveness of the overall UN effort in Romania. They are therefore an important element
in the formulation of the UNDAF and in the achievement of its objectives.
5. THE UNDAF: THE PROPOSED UN SYSTEM RESPONSE TO ROMANIA’s
PRIORITIES
a. Common Objectives
39. It became clear that the UNDAF exercise in Romania needed to focus on the
particular problems of Romania as a country in transition, especially how to create a
market economy and democratic society in the face of considerable social costs. It has
become clear that the legacy of the former authoritarian system in Romania created special
and unique difficulties for society and people to reorient their outlook and functioning to
the new realities.
40. Taking account of these special problems of transition, human rights in their
widest sense, particularly the right to development, have emerged as the principal common
issue for the Funds, Programmes and Specialized Agencies participating in the formulation
of the UNDAF in Romania. UN organisations, within their existing mandates and
programmes, pursue a rights-based approach to development and social inclusion of15
vulnerable groups (children, women, the elderly and the poor). With this focus in mind,
three main objectives have been identified:
1. Safeguard and Improve the Quality of Life of the People;
2. Accelerate the Country’s Transition to a well-governed Democratic Society;
3. Promote Environmental and Natural Resources Sustainability;
41. With respect to the first objective, to Safeguard and Improve the Quality of Life of
the People, it was recognised that poverty is a major cause of the Government’s inability to
protect some of the human rights of the people, particularly as they relate to basic needs in
the areas of health, education, nutrition, housing, sanitation, environment and access to
employment. The social dislocation resulting from the transition has disrupted the social
protection system. This especially affects vulnerable groups such as large families, the
disabled, women, children (particularly those who are institutionalised), the elderly and
minorities. A wide range of activity areas relevant to UN system priorities correspond to
this objective, such as:
- alleviating poverty;
- improving social safety nets;
- promoting gender equity;
- reforming the health system, women’s and children’s health, reproductive
health and family planning;
- helping children in especially difficult circumstances;
- reforming the education system;
- planning, social policy development and analysis;
- supporting SME’s and restructuring enterprises;
- promoting trade.
42. This first objective represents the main focus of the UN in Romania and presents
the best potential for a coordinated and joint effort of the UN system, where current and
future programmes of the different UN organisations can link up.
43. The second objective, to Accelerate the Country’s Transition to a Well-governed
Democratic Society, aims at helping Romania more rapidly achieve the transition to a
democratic society with transparent and accountable governance, that respects human
rights in their widest sense. This will require further transformation of governmental
institutions, to ensure administrative accountability and citizens’ empowerment, and
setting out policies and procedures with respect to civil servants. Another important
activity is reinforcement of and capacity building for civil society in all its forms, to help it16
through the early stages of development. The UN’s increasing emphasis on and experience
with governance should enable it to make a meaningful contribution towards this objective.
44. The third objective is to Promote Environmental and Natural Resources
Sustainability. The UN is currently focusing on three areas, namely disaster mitigation,
energy efficiency to reduce pollution, and regional environmental activities related to the
Danube and the Black Sea. In the future this emphasis will shift to aspects of the
environment which will have a more direct affect on people’s lives, such as safe drinking
water and sanitation. It will thus relate more closely to the objective of improving people’s
quality of life.
b. Strategic Approaches
45. To help achieve the above objectives, the UN system in Romania will employ the
following strategies:
- Advocacy
- National capacity building
- Strengthening civil society
- Partnerships and participation
- Preserving equity by targeting the most needy
- Models of excellence
- Provision of services
- Programme approach
- Regional networking
- Facilitating resource mobilisation and donor coordination
46. Advocacy is one of the main strategies for the entire UN system. It is directed first
and foremost to the promotion of values, attitudes and actions favourable to the realisation
of human rights, emphasising that development goals are based on the rights of all
members of society. UN interventions should influence policy development and
legislation, to promote compliance with international conventions concerning human
rights. Also, human rights issues should be mainstreamed in all UN system activities.
Advocacy for human rights and sustainable human development is particularly important
in the Romanian context.
47. National capacity building also constitutes a key strategy for the whole UN
system. It extends to institutions of government and of civil society, and to individual
decision makers. Special efforts will be made to build capacity for meeting the
commitments of the UN Global Conferences, through strengthened ability to deliver17
efficient and effective programmes for the target populations and promoting their
participation in them.
48. Strengthening civil society, and thereby empowering the citizens, is particularly
important in a country in transition like Romania, where the former political system
discouraged civil society development. As the role of the state is reduced, civil society
must play an increasingly active role. UN organisations have experience working with
NGO’s to meet development objectives. Citizens must participate/be empowered to play a
more active role in the design and implementation of programmes and policies that directly
affect their lives.
49. Preserving equity by targeting the most needy is particularly important in presentday Romania, to prevent vulnerable groups including women, children, disabled, elderly
and minorities from suffering excessively from the ongoing transition process.
50. Models of excellence enable countries to benefit from experiences elsewhere and
adopt the best practices. They frequently begin with pilot projects, which can later be
replicated on a larger scale, preferably without external support.
51. Partnerships and participation will be essential in forging strategic alliances which
contribute to social change. They will extend to all elements of civil society including local
communities, the private sector, religious groups, media and other actors for development
and, on the government side, planning and administrative agencies at local levels.
Partnerships with international financial institutions and other donors will also help realise
UNDAF goals.
52. Provision of services and technical assistance also support the government and
civil society, and supplement the activities of other donors. They can be instrumental in
assisting with project formulation, monitoring and evaluation, and strengthening capacity
for implementation and delivery of projects and programmes.
53. The Programme approach involves integrating UN system support as far as
possible into national development programmes. It involves taking an overall
programmatic view of the country’s development priorities in a certain sector or
programme and identifying the foreign assistance requirements which can be covered by
various UN organisations (and other providers of assistance) in an optimal way, according
to their comparative advantage.
54. Regional networks constitute a means for sharing experience within a geographic
region. This can be especially relevant in the case of Romania, since it is part of a region
where a number of countries have been passing through comparable transition processes.
55. Facilitating resource mobilisation and donor coordination. The UN system can18
assist the Government and other key development actors to obtain access to supplementary
resources. The UN system can also play a supporting role for the Government, to facilitate
coordination between development assistance providers.
56. The application of these strategies will vary according to needs and circumstances,
and the individual UN organisations will select those they find most suitable, depending on
their effectiveness in achieving specific objectives. Some of the strategies, such as capacity
building and strengthening civil society, may also be pursued in their own right as part of
the system’s objectives.
c. UN Organisations in Support of UNDAF Objectives
57. The UN system in Romania is of relatively modest size and coverage. UNDP,
UNICEF, UNFPA and UNHCR maintain regular programmes and country (subregional in
UNFPA’s case) offices; UNESCO is represented by its European Centre for Higher
Education which also functions as a UNESCO office in Bucharest. WHO and ILO
maintain liaison offices. UN bodies which are not represented in Romania such as UNIDO,
UNCTAD, ITC, UNIFEM and UNOPS have limited activities not included in the UNDAF,
some of which are financed by UNDP. The World Bank and IMF have sizeable operations
in Romania and maintain local offices.
58. UN programmes and areas of focus do not significantly overlap, hence the number
of collaborative activities has been limited. Nevertheless, there are a number of
collaborative activities. UNDP, UNFPA, ILO and WHO have cooperated towards the
formulation and implementation of the Government’s poverty alleviation programme.
UNDP and UNIDO provided joint support for the promotion of small and medium-scale
enterprises. UNICEF and UNFPA are jointly implementing women’s health activities,
UNDP and UNIFEM cooperate on economic empowerment of rural women and a new
anti-corruption programme has been developed by UNDP and the Centre for International
Crime Prevention. UNFPA and UNICEF contributed towards the production of the UNDPsupported National Human Development Reports.
59. At the same time, under the leadership of the Resident Coordinator, regular
contacts and cooperation have grown in several ways in recent years and are now well
established. A number of joint consultations (some as follow-up to UN conferences) on
such subjects as gender, media, HIV/AIDS, and human rights were held and a joint
newsletter has been published.
60. At the time of UNDAF formulation, the programmes of the UN organisations are
focused as follows:19
- UNAIDS, in addition to its main coordinating function, also has its own limited
programme of support in the area of HIV / AIDS.
- UNDP’s country framework (1997-2000) focuses on: Support to Governance,
Democracy and Participation which includes: governance, capacity building for
European integration, human development analysis and capacity building,
external resources management, and information exchange on the Internet;
Poverty Reduction and the Promotion of Sustainable Livelihoods, including:
poverty alleviation, social safety nets, women and gender equity, small and
medium scale enterprises restructuring, trade promotion; Promotion of
Environmental and Natural Resources Sustainability, including: disaster
mitigation, energy efficiency and management, regional environment programme.
- UNFPA helps implement the Programme of Action of the International
Conference on Population and Development (ICPD), with special emphasis on
Support for Advocacy of ICPD goals with a focus on Reproductive Health,
Family Planning and Adolescents. This includes action to support the
Government to develop plans, programmes and projects and to monitor progress.
New activities are being initiated to raise awareness on reproductive rights.
UNFPA also promotes and supports NGO’s, as well as coordination and
international collaboration in the area of reproductive health and family planning.
- UNHCR’s programme focuses on protection of refugees’ rights as well as the
prevention and reduction of statelessness.
- UNICEF’s Master Plan of Operations (1995-1999) contains the following
programmes: Family Education Programe including early childhood
development, social work and nurses training; Children’s and Women’s Health
including nutrition, expanded programme on immunisation, acute respiratory
infections/control of diarrhoeal diseases, safe motherhood and HIV/AIDS and
adolescents health; Children in Difficult Cirucmstances Programme including
children and family at risk, integration of disabled children into the community,
integration of de-institutionalised children, children in conflict with law and street
children; Planning Social Policies Development and Advocacy Programme
including social statistics and social policies.
- UNESCO, within the framework on its European Centre for Higher Education,
provides policy advice and limited support to Romania in this area as well as
support for regional cooperation.
- ILO provides general support through its liaison office. WHO maintains a regular
programme (bi-annual collaborative agreement on jointly agreed priority areas)20
coordinated by its Liaison Office. WHO’s priority areas include health policy
development, health care reform, women’s and children’s health, communicable
and non-communicable diseases, environment, and promotion of better health.

64. These areas of common interest will now be examined by corresponding interorganisation theme groups to identify new potential for cooperation. The theme groups
listed in table 4 were established on the basis of priority areas for UN collaboration and
cross-cutting subjects.22
65. In continuation of this detailed identification process, the UN country team
carefully considered various possibilities to intensify collaboration. There was consensus
that, if the UNDAF is to be an effective instrument for cooperation, specific mechanisms
of implementation should be established. After considerable discussion it was agreed to
proceed with the following actions:
- Each of the inter-organisation theme groups will be asked to prepare specific project
proposals for collaborative action. They will be reviewed by the Resident Coordinator
System, as well as by the Government.
- In view of their primary importance within the UNDAF, goal-oriented collaborative
activities focused on Poverty and Human Rights will be initiated on a priority basis.
With respect to the poverty proposal, possible concentration of collaborative activities
in a specific geographical area will be considered, in order to increase the potential
impact of the UN system intervention.
- In the long-term, programmes of individual UN organisations will be prepared with
the participation of concerned members of the system. This collaborative programming
is expected to contribute significantly toward identifying joint projects and programmes
in areas of common concern, and to maximise convergence within the UN system.

e. Monitoring and Evaluation
66. UNDAF progress needs to be systematically monitored using essentially the
existing structures, without imposing complicated new procedures, as UNDAF itself is not
adding to existing programmes.
67. Overall monitoring will be the task of the UN country team under the leadership of
the Resident Coordinator. Review of progress toward UNDAF objectives will be included
in their monthly meetings, and at least once a year a formal review will be undertaken23
involving also the representative of the Office of Prime Minister and Ministry of Foreign
Affairs. Results of this review will be reflected in the Resident Coordinator Annual Report.
68. The Heads of each team will be assisted in this task by the office of the Resident
Coordinator, which will draw appropriate subjects to their attention and provide relevant
information. This should include:
- monitoring and updating data in consultation with the National Commission for
Statistics;
- analysing trends and identifying problems;
- considering the status of the programmes of individual organiasations in
relation to UNDAF objectives;
- reviewing objectives, where necessary in conjunction with Government and
other international donors.
69. At the technical level, with respect to different sectors and areas of operation,
monitoring will be performed by the seven inter-organisation theme groups, which will
meet regularly to discuss operations and cooperation in their area of interest.
70. Finally, monitoring of UNDAF progress will be undertaken by each organisation in
conjunction with its own monitoring procedures. UNDAF criteria should become a
standard addition to each monitoring exercise, the results of which should be shared with
other members of the UN family.
71. The final criterion by which the UNDAF must be judged is its effectiveness in
serving to bring UN operations in the country closer together wherever possible, and
whenever this results in added value for the country.
